subject: Archaeology
title: Potassium-Argon Dating: Deep Time
description: A fast breakdown of Potassium-Argon Dating: Deep Time for builders.

hook.text: Radiocarbon dating stops working after 50,000 years. For older sites, scientists use volcanoes as their clock.

buildup.text: Potassium in volcanic rock decays into argon gas. The gas gets trapped in cooled lava, and its amount reveals the age.

discovery.text: This method dated the oldest human ancestors. The volcanic ash above and below Lucy placed her at 3.2 million years old.

twist.text: It only works on volcanic layers, not the fossils themselves. You date the rock sandwich around the find.

climax.text: Potassium-argon dating proved humans evolved in Africa millions of years ago — the evidence that settled the origin.

punchline.text: Volcanoes set the clock. Fossils just happened to be in between the eruptions.

quiz.question: How does potassium-argon dating work?
options: It measures potassium levels in fossilized bone tissue
It measures argon gas trapped in volcanic rock that formed around fossils
It tracks potassium decay in ancient pottery and metal tools
